interactions.label: Blue-green vomitus in a suspected case of poisoning is considered pathognomonic

params.question: Blue-green vomitus in a suspected case of poisoning is considered pathognomonic of which substance?

answers.text: Arsenic trioxide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Arsenic causes profuse rice-water diarrhoea resembling cholera, not blue-green vomitus. Blue-green colour is specific to copper sulphate crystals dissolving in gastric contents.

answers.text: Copper sulphate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Copper sulphate produces brilliant blue crystals that dissolve to give characteristic blue-green vomitus — essentially pathognomonic and one of the most reliable colour-based identifiers in forensic toxicology.

answers.text: Yellow phosphorus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Yellow phosphorus produces luminescent vomit that may glow faintly in the dark, not blue-green vomitus. Its identifying feature is the garlic odour and phosphorescent glow.

answers.text: Iodine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Iodine causes blue-black staining of mucous membranes on contact, not blue-green vomitus. The staining results from iodine's corrosive interaction with mucosal tissue.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the colour-based identification of poisons. Blue-green vomitus is pathognomonic of copper sulphate. Other poisons produce different colour signatures — luminescent vomit (phosphorus), blue-black staining (iodine), or rice-water stools (arsenic).
Well done. Blue-green vomitus from copper sulphate is one of the most visually distinctive signs in clinical toxicology and a reliable bedside identifier.

interactions.label: A patient develops ascending flaccid paralysis with profound hypokalaemia, yet t

params.question: A patient develops ascending flaccid paralysis with profound hypokalaemia, yet total body potassium is normal. Which mechanism best explains this presentation?

answers.text: Direct corrosive injury to peripheral nerves

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Corrosive injury (as seen with iodine) causes local tissue destruction, not selective hypokalaemia with preserved total body potassium. The dissociation between serum and total body K⁺ points to a channel-blocking mechanism.

answers.text: Blockade of potassium channels trapping K⁺ inside cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Soluble barium salts block inward-rectifier potassium channels, trapping K⁺ intracellularly. Plasma K⁺ drops sharply despite normal total body stores, producing ascending flaccid paralysis that can mimic Guillain-Barré syndrome. IV potassium chloride is the treatment.

answers.text: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition (seen with organophosphates) produces cholinergic excess — miosis, salivation, and fasciculations — not isolated hypokalaemia with flaccid paralysis.

answers.text: Fatty degeneration of anterior horn cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fatty degeneration affects the liver in phosphorus poisoning, not motor neurones. The key diagnostic clue here is the dissociation between low serum K⁺ and normal total body potassium — a pattern unique to barium.

overallFeedback.feedback: Barium's unique mechanism is K⁺ channel blockade — potassium is trapped inside cells, so serum K⁺ drops while total body K⁺ remains normal. This produces ascending flaccid paralysis that mimics Guillain-Barré. Remember: barium sulphate (used in radiology) is insoluble and safe; only soluble salts are toxic.
Excellent. Recognising this serum-vs-total-body potassium dissociation is the key to distinguishing barium poisoning from Guillain-Barré syndrome and other causes of ascending paralysis.

interactions.label: Why is British Anti-Lewisite (BAL) absolutely contraindicated as a chelator in i

params.question: Why is British Anti-Lewisite (BAL) absolutely contraindicated as a chelator in iron poisoning?

answers.text: It precipitates iron salts in the renal tubules, causing acute tubular necrosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: BAL does not precipitate iron in the kidneys. The actual danger is more insidious — it creates a lipid-soluble complex that crosses into the central nervous system.

answers.text: It forms a fat-soluble iron complex that redistributes into the central nervous system

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. BAL chelates iron into a lipophilic complex that crosses the blood-brain barrier, worsening CNS toxicity rather than reducing it. Deferoxamine is the correct chelator — vin rosé urine confirms it is working.

answers.text: It competitively inhibits deferoxamine, preventing effective chelation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: BAL does not interact with deferoxamine pharmacologically. The contraindication arises because BAL itself forms a dangerous fat-soluble iron complex that is neurotoxic.

answers.text: It accelerates haemolysis by destabilising the red cell membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haemolysis is a feature of copper sulphate poisoning, not a consequence of BAL–iron interaction. BAL is contraindicated in iron poisoning specifically because its iron complex is lipophilic and redistributes into the brain.

overallFeedback.feedback: BAL forms a fat-soluble complex with iron that crosses the blood-brain barrier, redistributing iron into the CNS and worsening toxicity. This is why deferoxamine — not BAL — is the chelator for iron poisoning. BAL remains appropriate for arsenic and mercury.
Well done. This is an absolute contraindication — BAL makes iron poisoning worse by driving iron into the CNS. Deferoxamine is the only appropriate chelator for iron.

interactions.label: You are collecting forensic specimens from a suspected poisoning victim in casua

params.question: You are collecting forensic specimens from a suspected poisoning victim in casualty. Which practice is most critical for ensuring the evidence remains admissible in court?

answers.text: Collecting gastric washings only after completing lavage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gastric aspirate should be collected before lavage begins — the first aspirate through the nasogastric tube is the highest-priority, time-limited specimen. Post-lavage washings are secondary.

answers.text: Using a grey-topped fluoride-oxalate tube for all blood specimens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Grey-topped tubes are correct for ethanol and volatile substances, but not for all analytes. Carbon monoxide specimens require a sealed glass tube because carboxyhaemoglobin vaporises from open containers. Tube selection must match the analyte.

answers.text: Labelling every specimen at the bedside before it leaves the collection device

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A specimen labelled later from memory is challengeable in court. Each label must carry the patient's name, number, date, time, and specimen type. Both the doctor and the police officer sign at handover, and every subsequent transfer requires a countersignature.

answers.text: Storing all specimens together in a single tamper-evident bag

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Each specimen must be individually sealed and labelled. Combining specimens in a single container risks cross-contamination — a procedural error that the defence can exploit to challenge admissibility.

overallFeedback.feedback: The most critical practice is labelling every specimen at the bedside, before it leaves the collection device. A specimen labelled from memory later is legally challengeable. The chain of custody — from bedside labelling through police handover with dual signatures — is what makes forensic evidence admissible.
Exactly right. Bedside labelling is the foundation of chain of custody. Without it, even perfectly collected specimens become inadmissible.

interactions.label: In a medicolegal report for suspected phosphorus poisoning, which entry correctl

params.question: In a medicolegal report for suspected phosphorus poisoning, which entry correctly demonstrates the separation of observation from inference?

answers.text: Writing 'phosphorus poisoning confirmed' under examination findings

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This places a conclusion in the observation section — exactly the cross-examination trap. Confirmation of the causative agent is an inference and belongs only in the opinion section.

answers.text: Writing 'the liver was enlarged and tender' under examination findings and 'findings are consistent with phosphorus poisoning' under the opinion section

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The raw observation (enlarged, tender liver) belongs in examination findings; the toxicological interpretation belongs in the opinion. This separation protects the report from cross-examination, where defence counsel specifically targets conclusions that have migrated into the observation sections.

answers.text: Writing 'garlic odour suggestive of phosphorus' under general examination

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While garlic odour is a valid observation, appending 'suggestive of phosphorus' imports inference into the findings section. The correct approach is to record 'garlic odour on breath' as the finding and place the interpretation in the opinion.

answers.text: Writing 'copper sulphate lavage was administered as this is a case of phosphorus poisoning' under treatment in the examination section

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This embeds a diagnostic conclusion ('this is a case of phosphorus poisoning') within the treatment record. Treatment facts belong in the report, but their diagnostic rationale belongs in the opinion section where the examining doctor writes as an expert, not a witness.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle: raw observations (what you saw, heard, measured) go in the examination findings; their toxicological meaning goes in the opinion. A finding in the wrong section can unravel a case under cross-examination. The examining doctor is both witness (recording observations) and expert (interpreting them) — the report must keep these roles separated.

Excellent. Maintaining this observation–inference boundary is the examining doctor's most critical forensic obligation. Cross-examination specifically targets conclusions that have drifted into the wrong section.
